newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Tanzanian coffee expert sets production target.
newsitem.headline: Tanzanian coffee expert sets production target.

text.p: Tanzania's annual coffee production, in decline and handicapped by drought, ageing trees and poor husbandry, could be restored to 60,000 tonnes per year in under five years, a senior industry figure said.

Jeremy Lefroy, managing director of the Moshi-based African Coffee Company (ACC), told Reuters at the weekend it was his goal to see the 60,000 tonne target attained and listing five preconditions in order to achieve the objective.

Lefroy sits on the Tanzania Coffee Board (TCB) and is secretary of the Tanzania Coffee Association (TCA), formed in February as the lead industry voice. Its members include local traders, exporters, growers, cooperatives and agents.
At its peak in the mid 1980s, Tanzania produced around 68,000 tonnes of coffee a year with production averaging 55,160 tonnes between 1981-85.

However, production has slumped over the past decade with the 1996/97 (October/September) season forecast between 41-43,000 tonnes worth about $90 million. This compares with 53,000 tonnes in the 1995/96 crop year.

Tanzanian coffee is the country's agricultural mainstay with premium quality mild-washed arabicas grown around the foothills of Mount Kilimanjaro accounting for 50 percent of the country's arabica coffee which in turn accounts for 75 percent of total Tanzanian coffee output.

Lefroy listed the five preconditions as an increase in coffee seedling production, farmer education, inputs, research and development of diseases resistant coffee trees and the rehabilitation of estates and farms.
"If we go for all these five (conditions) then we could see Tanzania back up to 60,000 tonnes in under five years," he said.
A key element in the fight-back strategy to restore production involves a massive replanting scheme to replace the bulk of the country's ageing arabica coffee trees.
In the northern zone, most of the trees are about 50-60 years old, well past their productive prime, while some are 100 years old and date back to the German colonial period.

Lefroy said farmers should be encouraged to replant at least five percent of their trees every season."I would like to see five percent of the coffee trees replanted for the next twenty years -- ideally ten percent.
"Our aim would be to see 60 million trees replaced over the next 10 to 20 years. If we could replant 60 (million) then we get Tanzania back to 60,000 tonnes per annum," he said.
High-level industry sources said that Tanzania is capable of producing in excess of 100,000 tonnes of coffee per year.
Tanzania's arabica coffee is well-regarded and enjoys a reputation of being among the world's best, traders said.
"It is considered one of the top three coffees in Japan. There is progress being made on quality and this is reflected in premiums over the New York market," Lefroy said.
The ACC and coffee house C.Dorman are looking at a joint venture to rehabilitate several coffee farms in the Kilimanjaro region, Lefroy said.
"This country used to have a reputation for producing among the world's best coffee. It can still get there but it will take some time," said a senior official from C.Dorman.

About 90 percent of Tanzania's coffee is grown on small holdings averaging half to one hectare. Arabica production involves some 20,000 families who usually interplant their crop with bananas as an added source of cash.
Tanzania's arabica coffee is thought to have been first introduced in the 1890s by Jesuit priests from Reunion Island in the Indian Ocean.
